newsitem.title: SPAIN: Disney in talks to build Spanish theme park.
newsitem.headline: Disney in talks to build Spanish theme park.

text.p: U.S. entertainment giant Walt Disney Co is among several groups negotiating to build a new theme park on the eastern coast of Spain, a local official said on Friday.
The regional government of Valencia is in talks with Disney, Paramount and Universal Studios over plans to build a large theme park near the sun and sea resort region of Alicante.

"The regional president Eduardo Zaplana went to the U.S. with a delegation last week and met company heads, including at Disney, to discuss the construction of a theme park in the south of the region," a local government spokeswoman told Reuters.
The exact location of the theme park had not been decided but it will be in the province of Alicante, near the popular Costa Blanca tourist resort of the same name.

"We still don't know what type of park it would be and negotiations now centre on whether it would be better to build it together with one of the large groups or give it its own name, like Port Aventura," the official said.

The Spanish delegation met Disney officials in Orlando, Florida, last Thursday including the multinational's Spanish partner. They also met former Disney vice-chairman Steven Backer, now a theme park consultant.
If Disney went ahead with the park, it would be its second European venture after Disneyland Paris. Spain was considered as a location for the project during initial talks.

The French leisure complex has had a rocky start and the outlook is still shaky although it is expected to make a profit in 1996 for the second year in a row. Rainy weather and a strong French franc have helped dampen sales.

If Valencia goes ahead with the construction of its own theme park, it would enter into direct competition with nearby Port Aventura, a $500 million theme park south of Barcelona which opened last year.
Port Aventura, majority-owned by British media group Pearson, has beaten forecasts by attracting thousands of visitors lured by warm southern temperatures and nearby beaches.

Spain is the world's second most popular tourist destination after France with more than 45 million visitors in 1995. Tourism revenue makes up nine percent of Spain's gross domestic product and accounts for 11 percent of jobs.
